title: The Tale of Genji
objective: After this level you can explain why Murasaki Shikibu's Tale of Genji is often called the world's first novel.
summary: Murasaki Shikibu, a court lady, finished The Tale of Genji about 1010. Hiragana let Heian women write, and its 54 chapters of inner life are why it's often called the first novel.

cards.headline: About 1010, a court lady finished what's often called the first novel.
cards.body: She was Murasaki Shikibu, and she wrote The Tale of Genji while serving at the Japanese court. Why does a book that old get that title? Start with who got to write what.

cards.headline: The script that let women write
cards.body: We don't know her real name. We do know she learned Chinese, then generally the exclusive sphere of men. At the Heian court, men composed official documents in stilted Chinese. Hiragana, a script for writing Japanese, gave court women their chance to create works of literature. The men kept the official language. The women got the stories.

cards.headline: One life, 54 chapters
cards.body: Genji follows one character and his legacy through 54 chapters. The hero is a handsome, sensitive, gifted courtier, an excellent lover and a worthy friend. The book shows supreme sensitivity to human emotions and to nature, and as it goes on, its tone darkens, reflecting the Buddhist conviction that this world doesn't last. A long story that follows inner lives over time: that's what a novel does.

mascot.line: Keep the hedge: Genji is often called the first novel. Scholars argue about firsts, so say it that way too.

cards.headline: From heroes to people
cards.body: Remember Level 1: the epic lifts its heroes up, while the novel often shows life as unheroic and imperfect. Genji fights no monsters. He's a lover and a friend at court, and the book is an absorbing picture of Heian aristocrats: their entertainment, dress, daily life and moral code. A hero's story with the heroics left out.
